title: Cost transparency deep dive (model/region) - Redwood Inference x Ironclad Systems
summary: Ironclad asked for cost transparency by model and region for an enterprise evaluation (Dedicated + possible VPC). Redwood walked through how they internally compute “blended cost per 1M output tokens” (compute + overhead allocations, cache/batching impacts, credits/discount policy separation) and how the internal unit economics dashboard reconciles to billing/metering. Customer’s key asks were (1) ability to export daily cost trends by model/region/tier, (2) clarity on what’s included vs excluded (training, support, idle capacity), and (3) how routing/fallback and caching change unit cost. Redwood described current internal dashboards and a path to make a subset customer-facing (likely via scheduled exports and later Console views), with caveats around multi-tenant signals, discounts, and security/RBAC.
topics: Definition of blended $/1M output tokens and inclusions/exclusions
Cost breakdown by model family/variant and cloud region
Dedicated capacity vs hosted API economics (idle vs utilized GPU time)
Cache hit rate and batching effects on unit cost
Routing policies, fallbacks, and explaining cost deltas (mix shift vs runtime changes)
Reconciliation to billing/metering and variance tolerances
Security/RBAC for cost data and audit logs
questions: Can we see $/1M output tokens by model and by region on a daily basis, and export it?
What exactly is included in “blended” cost—does it include platform overhead, support, idle GPU time, credits/discounts?
How do you attribute cost when you do fallback routing across models or regions?
How do cache hits show up—do we see savings or just lower effective $/token?
For Dedicated, can we see utilization vs effective unit cost so FinOps can tie it to commits?
Can you commit to reconciliation accuracy vs invoices, and what’s the expected lag/late events behavior?
If this becomes customer-facing, how do you prevent leaking information across tenants?
action_items: Redwood (Nikhil): Send a one-pager describing Redwood’s “blended $/1M output tokens” definition (inclusions/exclusions) and reconciliation approach.
Redwood (Logan): Share a sample export format (CSV) for daily unit-cost by model + region + deployment tier (with dummy data).
Customer (Hannah): Provide Ironclad’s preferred regional breakdown (e.g., us-east-1, us-west-2, eu-west-1) and the models in scope for the pilot.
Customer (Evan): Share current request mix assumptions (avg output tokens, context sizes, streaming %) to sanity check unit-cost drivers.
Redwood (Vanessa): Confirm what parts of fleet overhead are included in the internal blended metric vs tracked separately for margin reporting.
Redwood (Nikhil): Schedule a follow-up to review a pilot plan and confirm reporting cadence (weekly vs daily) with FinOps + Security.
next_steps: Redwood to email blended metric definition + example export by end of week.
Ironclad to confirm pilot regions/models and whether they want Dedicated only or Dedicated + VPC option.
Schedule 45-min follow-up: “pilot scope + reporting + security review lite”.
transcript:
Meeting: Cost transparency deep dive (model/region) - Redwood Inference x Ironclad Systems
Recorded: 2025-01-22 19:00 UTC
Duration: 48 min
Attendees (Redwood): Nikhil Sharma, Logan Wright, Vanessa Ortiz
Attendees (Ironclad): Priya Deshmukh, Evan Miller, Hannah Cho, Markus Voss

---
Auto Summary (Fireflies)
- Customer evaluating Redwood Dedicated and asked for cost reporting broken down by model and region.
- Redwood explained internal unit economics dashboard approach and reconciliation to billing.
- Discussion covered cache/batching/quantization and routing/fallback impacts on unit cost.

Topics
1) What “blended cost per 1M output tokens” means
2) Regional and model granularity; exports
3) Dedicated vs hosted accounting (utilization)
4) Reconciliation, late metering events
5) Security/RBAC for cost data

Action items
- Redwood to send metric definition and sample export.
- Customer to share expected mix + target regions/models.

---

[00:00] Nikhil Sharma: Cool, thanks everyone for the time. I know this is a little more in the weeds than the usual first call. Priya, you wanted this to be mostly about cost transparency, right?

[00:11] Priya Deshmukh: Yeah. We can do model evals ourselves. The blocker internally is: if we move off, like, Bedrock and Azure OpenAI, our finance team is going to ask, “okay, show me by region, by model, what are we spending, what changed, why.” We need that.

[00:28] Hannah Cho: And we need it in a format we can ingest. Not screenshots.

[00:32] Nikhil Sharma: Yep, makes sense. I pulled Logan in—he runs our telemetry and analytics pipeline for this stuff—and Vanessa who owns the fleet cost inputs. So we can be precise.

[00:44] Logan Wright: Hey all.

[00:45] Vanessa Ortiz: Hi everyone.

[00:48] Evan Miller: Hey.

[00:49] Markus Voss: Hello.

[00:52] Nikhil Sharma: Maybe we start with the core metric. Internally we track “blended cost per one million output tokens.” I’m going to say output tokens a lot because input tokens can be… tricky depending on cache and prompts and retrieval. But we can do both.

[01:10] Hannah Cho: Output is what we care about, generally, because our product usage maps closer to that.

[01:15] Nikhil Sharma: Exactly.

[01:16] Priya Deshmukh: When you say “blended,” is that like fully-loaded cost? Or just GPU time?

[01:22] Logan Wright: Good question. Internally it’s compute plus allocated overhead. So it’s not only GPU seconds. It’s “what does it cost us to serve” including some shared platform overhead—control plane, base infra, oncall, stuff like that. But we’re explicit about what’s included.

[01:41] Hannah Cho: Does it include credits and discounts? Like, if we negotiate a discount, does that change the metric?

[01:48] Nikhil Sharma: For internal unit econ, we separate “cost” from “revenue.” Credits/discounts affect revenue side, margin, but not the underlying cost. That said, we can show you both views in reporting: effective price per 1M output tokens and cost per 1M output tokens.

[02:07] Vanessa Ortiz: And to be super clear, the blended cost number is computed from underlying cost inputs—GPU fleet costs, networking, storage, etc.—then allocated down to request aggregates using observed usage signals.

[02:20] Evan Miller: Observed usage signals meaning tokens and time?

[02:23] Logan Wright: Tokens, GPU time proxies, plus runtime configuration tags—batching, caching, quant profile. We don’t usually expose all of those externally today, but we capture them.

[02:35] Priya Deshmukh: Okay. Can we get that by model and by region though? Like literally a table: “Llama-3.1-70B” in “eu-west,” cost is X yesterday.

[02:46] Nikhil Sharma: That’s the ask, yes.

[02:48] Logan Wright: Our internal dashboard does exactly that: day, model variant, region, and “tier” which is like self-serve vs dedicated vs private. For you, it’d be dedicated, and possibly VPC if you go that route.

[03:06] Hannah Cho: You said “tier.” Is that like customer tier?

[03:10] Logan Wright: It’s an internal dimension that maps to the deployment mode and commercial construct. Hosted API multi-tenant, Dedicated reserved capacity, Private VPC/on-prem. Sometimes also an enterprise sub-tier because accounting differs.

[03:25] Markus Voss: If you expose reporting, we’ll need to understand access controls. Finance data is sensitive.

[03:31] Nikhil Sharma: Totally. We’ll get to that. We’ve implemented RBAC and audit logs for internal cost views, and if we make customer-facing reporting it would be scoped to your org, with strict roles.

[03:46] Priya Deshmukh: Before security, I want the data question. How do you reconcile this to the invoice? Because we’ve had issues where vendor dashboards don’t match the bill.

[03:55] Logan Wright: Yep, this is a big one. We run a reconciliation job daily that compares aggregated unit-econ totals to billing/metering totals. There is always some variance due to late events and backfills—so we define a tolerance. Internally we alert if variance is over a threshold.

[04:15] Hannah Cho: What threshold?

[04:17] Logan Wright: Typically low single-digit percent at daily granularity, and tighter at weekly/monthly once late events settle. The daily view can be noisy if a region has delayed metering.

[04:30] Evan Miller: Late events meaning the token counts come in late?

[04:33] Logan Wright: Metering events, yes. Sometimes ingestion lag, sometimes retries. Especially if there’s a partial outage. We mark partitions as “provisional” until they meet completeness checks.

[04:47] Nikhil Sharma: From a user perspective, the dashboard has a freshness indicator. It’s like: this day is 99% complete; treat it as final-ish, versus “still cooking.”

[04:58] Priya Deshmukh: That’s actually helpful.

[05:00] Hannah Cho: But for enterprise reporting, we need something we can trust, even if delayed. Like, “give me the final numbers for last week by Tuesday.”

[05:10] Nikhil Sharma: That’s a very reasonable requirement. We can talk about a reporting SLA for the export.

[05:16] Vanessa Ortiz: Also, on the cost input side, some costs are monthly invoices (cloud committed use, colo lease, etc.) that get allocated daily. So early-in-month can look slightly different until the month closes, depending on how you treat amortization. We treat it consistently, but I’m flagging it.

[05:38] Hannah Cho: Yeah, that’s fine as long as it’s consistent and documented.

[05:43] Priya Deshmukh: Can you walk through the formula? Like literally what’s in the numerator and denominator.

[05:49] Logan Wright: Sure. Denominator: total output tokens for the slice (day x model x region x tier). Numerator: compute cost attributed to those requests (GPU + related infra), plus allocated overhead cost for that slice. Then multiply to $ per 1M output tokens.

[06:12] Evan Miller: How do you attribute compute cost to a request? GPUs are shared across requests, continuous batching, etc.

[06:19] Logan Wright: Right, you can’t just say “this request used 3.2 seconds of GPU.” We do it at an aggregated level. We instrument runtime throughput and utilization per pool and model. We compute effective cost per generated token for that pool and allocate across requests. It’s basically “pool cost * share of token work” after adjusting for idle time.

[06:43] Priya Deshmukh: Adjusting for idle time is important. Because on Dedicated, if we pay for a reserved pool, idle time is on us.

[06:51] Nikhil Sharma: Exactly. So the cost reporting needs to show two things for Dedicated: (1) “effective unit cost” including idle, and (2) “marginal unit cost” when utilized.

[07:03] Hannah Cho: Yes. That’s how we do it in FinOps.

[07:06] Vanessa Ortiz: Internally we track utilization and capacity efficiency. For Dedicated we can provide both views so you can manage your commit.

[07:16] Evan Miller: For hosted multi-tenant, do you also include idle?

[07:19] Logan Wright: Idle exists but it’s amortized across tenants and handled in our blended metric. For customer-facing, we’d likely present “effective price” rather than our internal cost.

[07:31] Priya Deshmukh: Understood. For our needs, we want to see “what did we spend” and “why did it change.” So, can you do a driver breakdown? Like model mix shift vs region mix shift.

[07:44] Nikhil Sharma: That’s actually part of what we’re building internally right now—the “explain” panel. It attributes deltas to drivers: region mix, model mix, cache hit rate changes, quant profile adoption, routing changes.

[07:58] Hannah Cho: Is that available to customers?

[08:00] Nikhil Sharma: Not today as a product feature. But we can provide it in the pilot as a managed report. Longer term, we’re considering a customer-facing subset in Console.

[08:13] Evan Miller: How would routing show up? Say you fallback from model A to model B.

[08:18] Logan Wright: We tag requests with the “served model” and also the “requested model,” plus route policy when available. So you can measure: you asked for X, but we served Y because of capacity or policy.

[08:33] Priya Deshmukh: You said “when available.” That’s a red flag.

[08:36] Logan Wright: Sorry, let me clarify. It’s available in our telemetry for our stack. When a customer uses our API directly, we have it. If you’re integrating via some gateway and not passing route tags, you could lose fidelity. But in a Dedicated deployment, we control the routing plane, so it’s there.

[08:56] Nikhil Sharma: And we can make sure the contract includes those tags, so reporting is consistent.

[09:02] Markus Voss: On tagging: are there any customer identifiers in the telemetry? If you’re exporting to us, we need to ensure it’s only our data.

[09:11] Nikhil Sharma: Yes, tenant scoping is strict. For Dedicated it’s physically isolated anyway. For hosted, we use org IDs. Export would be filtered at query time and access-controlled.

[09:23] Markus Voss: And audit logs? Who accessed what report.

[09:26] Nikhil Sharma: Yep. We can provide audit logs for console access. For exports, we can log generation and delivery.

[09:35] Hannah Cho: Back to the model/region breakdown. What’s the grain? Daily is fine, but can we do hourly when we’re debugging spikes?

[09:43] Logan Wright: Internally we aggregate daily for unit econ as the stable truth. Hourly is possible but higher variance and more late-data issues. For debugging, we usually pair daily cost with near-real-time operational metrics: tokens per second, error rate, cache hits, etc.

[10:02] Evan Miller: Cache hits—how do those factor into unit cost?

[10:06] Logan Wright: If you have prefix caching or KV cache reuse, the effective compute per output token goes down, because you spend less compute per token generated, depending on how you structure prompts. We measure cache hit rate and estimate savings. In the unit econ view, you’ll see lower $/1M output tokens when cache hit rate improves.

[10:27] Priya Deshmukh: But do you show savings explicitly? Like “cache saved $X.”

[10:31] Logan Wright: Internally we do an estimated savings column. It’s modeled, not perfect. It’s “counterfactual cost without cache” minus “actual.”

[10:41] Hannah Cho: Modeled is okay as long as it’s labeled.

[10:44] Nikhil Sharma: Exactly. We’d label it “estimate.”

[10:48] Evan Miller: What about batching? If we increase batching, latency might go up but cost goes down.

[10:53] Nikhil Sharma: Yup. That’s the classic trade. Our runtime uses continuous batching, and we can tune. Reporting-wise, we capture the runtime config / batching profile so you can correlate unit cost with config changes.

[11:08] Priya Deshmukh: So you’re basically saying you already have an internal dashboard that does all of this.

[11:13] Logan Wright: For internal, yes. It’s used by product and finance. The question is packaging it safely for customers.

[11:22] Hannah Cho: What’s the timeline on that? Because we can’t go to procurement with “trust us.”

[11:28] Nikhil Sharma: For the evaluation/pilot, we can commit to providing a scheduled export—CSV or Parquet—daily, broken down by model and region. That’s doable now with some manual glue. Productizing into Console is a roadmap item.

[11:46] Priya Deshmukh: Scheduled export to where?

[11:49] Nikhil Sharma: We can drop to your S3 bucket, or email is… not ideal. Prefer S3/GCS with KMS.

[11:57] Markus Voss: S3 with our KMS and IAM role is fine.

[12:02] Evan Miller: Also, can you include token counts and request counts? Otherwise it’s hard to sanity check.

[12:08] Logan Wright: Absolutely. We include: output tokens, input tokens, request count, cache hit rate (if applicable), and the unit cost metric.

[12:19] Hannah Cho: Is region the cloud region like “eu-west-1” or your internal region names?

[12:24] Logan Wright: Both. We normalize to canonical names. There have been issues in the past when mapping changed, so we maintain a mapping table with historical correctness.

[12:36] Priya Deshmukh: Historical correctness meaning if you rename a region you don’t rewrite history.

[12:40] Logan Wright: Exactly.

[12:42] Hannah Cho: Good.

[12:44] Nikhil Sharma: On the “why did it change” question: the export can include a driver view in V1, but it might be basic. Like, compare last 7 days vs previous 7, attribute to mix shifts.

[12:58] Priya Deshmukh: That’d be great. That’s what our execs want.

[13:01] Evan Miller: Can you explain how mix shift attribution works? Like what methodology.

[13:06] Logan Wright: It’s basically a decomposition. Keep unit costs per model/region fixed and change weights, then vice versa. So you can say “X% of delta from model mix, Y% from region mix, Z% from within-slice cost changes.”

[13:24] Evan Miller: So kind of a Shapley-ish thing?

[13:27] Logan Wright: Not full Shapley, no. More like stepwise decomposition. We can document it.

[13:34] Hannah Cho: Please document. Otherwise it becomes a debate.

[13:38] Nikhil Sharma: Yep.

[13:41] Markus Voss: Security question: if you’re allocating overhead, does that include other customers’ overhead? Like are we subsidizing multi-tenant stuff?

[13:50] Vanessa Ortiz: For Dedicated, overhead allocation is based on dedicated environment overhead, not multi-tenant. There’s some shared corporate overhead we track internally for margin, but for customer reporting we can keep it to “service overhead attributable to your deployment.”

[14:08] Markus Voss: Okay. We just need it clear.

[14:10] Priya Deshmukh: And for Private / VPC, would it be similar?

[14:14] Nikhil Sharma: Similar, yes, but cost visibility depends on whether you bring your own cloud account. If it’s in your VPC but our account, we can provide the same reporting. If it’s fully in your account, then you’d use your own cloud billing plus our metering.

[14:32] Evan Miller: We’d prefer it in our account long term, but for pilot we can do your account.

[14:37] Nikhil Sharma: That’s common.

[14:39] Hannah Cho: For the pilot, I want “blended $/1M output tokens” by model and region. But I also want to know how you compute it so we can compare to our internal numbers.

[14:50] Logan Wright: We can share the definition and a sample calculation. Some things we may not share are our exact cost inputs per GPU, but we can share structure.

[15:02] Hannah Cho: That’s fine. We don’t need your vendor rates, we need consistency.

[15:07] Nikhil Sharma: Also note: if you’re comparing to, say, Azure OpenAI, those numbers won’t match because their price is price, our metric is cost. But we can also show you effective price per 1M tokens in the contract.

[15:23] Priya Deshmukh: Right now our executive question is: “if we move to Dedicated, do we get predictable spend and do we have the levers.” So both cost and price matter.

[15:34] Nikhil Sharma: Makes sense.

[15:36] Evan Miller: Let’s talk about regions. We need EU data residency, at least eu-west. Maybe also Frankfurt. Can you break down if a request is served in a different region due to failover?

[15:49] Logan Wright: Yes, we record served region and requested region. In a failover, served region changes. That can be a driver of cost deltas as well.

[16:02] Priya Deshmukh: If that happens, is it opt-in? We might not allow cross-region.

[16:06] Nikhil Sharma: In Dedicated you can configure routing policy. If you need strict residency, we can do no cross-region failover, but then availability tradeoffs apply.

[16:17] Priya Deshmukh: Understood.

[16:18] Hannah Cho: For reporting, I need to see that. Because otherwise EU spend might get “mysteriously” low and US high.

[16:25] Nikhil Sharma: Exactly.

[16:28] Evan Miller: You mentioned quantization profiles earlier. We’re sensitive about quality regression. If you change quant, unit cost goes down, but quality might drop.

[16:38] Nikhil Sharma: Yep, and we don’t want to optimize cost at the expense of output quality without guardrails. Internally, we link quant profile tags to eval results. For customers, we can expose which profile is active per deployment and correlate to cost and latency.

[16:55] Evan Miller: Do you have a default? Like do you force quant for dedicated?

[16:58] Nikhil Sharma: No force. It’s configurable. We recommend profiles depending on your latency/cost target.

[17:05] Priya Deshmukh: If we do a canary rollout of a new profile, can reporting show before/after?

[17:10] Logan Wright: Yes, because the profile tag is a dimension. You could slice “profile A vs profile B” for the same model.

[17:19] Hannah Cho: But you said cardinality issues earlier. How many dimensions can you realistically support?

[17:25] Logan Wright: Great point. Internally, we cap what’s in the canonical dataset. Model, region, tier are always there. Runtime config and quant profile are optional and sometimes only available in deeper tables. For customer export, we should keep it limited: model, region, and maybe “deployment config version” which you control.

[17:46] Priya Deshmukh: That’s fine. We don’t need 50 columns.

[17:49] Evan Miller: I do want at least the ability to tie cost changes to config changes though.

[17:54] Nikhil Sharma: We can include a “config_id” or “rollout_id” in the export. That’s a good compromise.

[18:02] Evan Miller: Perfect.

[18:04] Markus Voss: Another security angle: if you’re exporting daily, are you putting any request-level data in it?

[18:09] Logan Wright: No, it’s aggregated. Daily aggregates. No prompts, no content.

[18:14] Markus Voss: Good.

[18:16] Hannah Cho: Can it be by customer tier? Like if we have multiple business units.

[18:22] Nikhil Sharma: We can do business unit separation if you set up separate projects or API keys. Then reporting can break down by project.

[18:33] Priya Deshmukh: We can do that.

[18:35] Evan Miller: Can I ask a dumb question: why output tokens, not total tokens?

[18:40] Logan Wright: Not dumb. Output tokens map more directly to compute cost in generation heavy workloads. Input tokens matter too, but caching can make input “cheaper” in practice, so output is often more stable for unit cost discussions. We still track both.

[18:59] Hannah Cho: For budgeting, we use total, but okay.

[19:02] Nikhil Sharma: We can add both to the export, plus show $/1M total tokens as a secondary metric.

[19:10] Priya Deshmukh: Great.

[19:12] Nikhil Sharma: Let me ask: what’s your current reporting from Bedrock/Azure like? What’s missing?

[19:18] Hannah Cho: Bedrock: we get region spend from AWS billing, but not by model in a clean way, and it’s delayed. Azure: we get usage but the mapping from model deployment to internal cost center is messy. Also, when the product team changes model routing, finance finds out weeks later.

[19:39] Priya Deshmukh: And we want proactive alerts if cost per token spikes.

[19:44] Nikhil Sharma: Yep. Internally we alert on regressions in $/1M tokens. For customer-facing, we could do a webhook or email alert if your unit cost deviates beyond threshold.

[19:57] Evan Miller: That’s awesome.

[19:58] Hannah Cho: Careful. Awesome if it’s accurate.

[20:01] Logan Wright: (laughs) Fair.

[20:03] Nikhil Sharma: We’d start simple: weekly review and an agreed baseline.

[20:08] Priya Deshmukh: You said you’re building this internally. Is it stable? We don’t want to be guinea pigs.

[20:14] Logan Wright: It’s already used internally as source of truth. We’re standardizing definitions and improving drilldowns, plus reconciliation automation. The export would be based on that.

[20:26] Hannah Cho: Okay.

[20:27] Evan Miller: On reconciliation: if we see a variance, do we have a way to debug? Like, is there a “provisional” flag.

[20:34] Logan Wright: Yes. Each day/region slice has completeness and freshness markers. We can include those in export: “data_status=provisional/final” and “completeness_pct.”

[20:50] Hannah Cho: Great.

[20:52] Priya Deshmukh: Can we talk about dedicated commit. If we reserve, say, 8x H100s in eu-west, how would unit cost be reported? Because early on we’ll have low utilization.

[21:05] Vanessa Ortiz: You’d see higher effective $/1M output tokens at low utilization. That’s expected. We can also show a utilization metric so you can separate “waste” from “efficiency.”

[21:18] Hannah Cho: That’s what I want.

[21:20] Evan Miller: Do you have a notion of “idle cost” separately?

[21:23] Vanessa Ortiz: Internally, yes. For a customer export, we could include: total cost, utilized cost, idle cost. But we need to be careful not to expose too much pricing-sensitive internal structure. For Dedicated, it’s your pool, so it’s less sensitive.

[21:43] Priya Deshmukh: I’d argue it’s essential for dedicated.

[21:46] Nikhil Sharma: Agreed. We can include it.

[21:48] Markus Voss: If it’s in an export, we need to ensure it doesn’t contain Redwood internal secrets.

[21:53] Nikhil Sharma: Understood. We’ll keep it to your environment metrics.

[21:58] Evan Miller: How do you handle overhead allocation in Dedicated? Like control plane overhead.

[22:03] Vanessa Ortiz: There’s a small fixed overhead and some variable. For Dedicated we attribute the fixed overhead to the deployment as a constant daily cost and variable overhead based on usage. We can provide a simplified view: “platform overhead” as a line item.

[22:23] Hannah Cho: Perfect. That’s what our CFO expects.

[22:26] Priya Deshmukh: Okay, so roadmap. You said customer-facing in Console is not available. What do we get now?

[22:34] Nikhil Sharma: For pilot: daily export to your S3, plus a weekly review template where we summarize drivers. Optionally a read-only view in Console behind a feature flag if we’re comfortable.

[22:48] Priya Deshmukh: If it’s behind a feature flag, I’m fine, as long as it’s stable.

[22:52] Logan Wright: We can do it. But we’ll likely start with export, because it’s less UI work.

[22:58] Hannah Cho: Export is fine.

[23:00] Evan Miller: One more question: can you break down by endpoint type? Chat vs embeddings vs rerank.

[23:06] Logan Wright: For token-based metrics, chat/text generation is primary. For embeddings we track cost per 1M embedding tokens or per 1K requests depending. In the dataset, there’s a “route_type.” We can include it, but again, cardinality. If it’s important, we can.

[23:23] Priya Deshmukh: For now, generation only is okay. We’ll expand later.

[23:27] Hannah Cho: Agree.

[23:29] Nikhil Sharma: Great. Let’s do this: you tell us the models and regions you care about. We’ll send a sample export schema and the metric definition doc. Then we schedule a follow-up to lock pilot scope and reporting SLA.

[23:44] Priya Deshmukh: Works.

[23:45] Evan Miller: I’ll send the model list. Probably two: a 70B-ish model and a smaller one for cheap calls.

[23:51] Nikhil Sharma: Cool.

[23:52] Hannah Cho: And I’ll send the region list and desired tags.

[23:56] Markus Voss: I’ll send security requirements for the S3 integration and who can access.

[24:02] Nikhil Sharma: Perfect.

[24:04] Logan Wright: One thing to flag: if you do cross-region failover disabled, cost variability might be higher during incidents. But reporting will show it.

[24:13] Priya Deshmukh: That’s fine. We’ll make the trade.

[24:16] Nikhil Sharma: Any other questions before we wrap?

[24:18] Hannah Cho: Just: can you commit that the export ties out to invoice within some tolerance?

[24:25] Nikhil Sharma: We can commit to a reconciliation tolerance and a finalization window (e.g., daily numbers may be provisional for 24–48 hours). We’ll put that in writing for the pilot.

[24:38] Hannah Cho: Great.

[24:39] Evan Miller: And can you include request count and average output length? That helps debug.

[24:44] Logan Wright: Yes. Request_count and avg_output_tokens are easy.

[24:50] Nikhil Sharma: Alright, we’ll follow up via email with the docs and next meeting options.

[24:55] Priya Deshmukh: Thanks.

[24:56] Hannah Cho: Thanks.

[24:57] Evan Miller: Thanks.

[24:58] Markus Voss: Thank you.

(Recording ends abruptly)
